pos: n. (the designation of Adino, chief among David's captains; named once)
etymology: A gentilic of uncertain origin, Hebrew 'Etsni, perhaps connected with chanith, a spear, and so a spearman; named once, 2 Samuel 23:8.
biblical_def: Eznite occurs once, in the opening verse of the roll of David's mighty men: “These be the names of the mighty men whom David had: The Tachmonite that sat in the seat, chief among the captains; the same was Adino the Eznite: he lift up his spear against eight hundred, whom he slew at one time” (2 Samuel 23:8). The verse is among the most heavily annotated in the Authorized Version, the translators' margin offering alternative readings for the chief's name and title, and the parallel in Chronicles gives him another name and a different figure: “And this is the number of the mighty men whom David had; Jashobeam, an Hachmonite, the chief of the captains: he lifted up his spear against three hundred slain by him at one time” (1 Chronicles 11:11). The dictionary notes both and resolves neither, because Scripture does not. What is plain is the man's place: first in a list of thirty-seven, which closes with a name no reader forgets: “Uriah the Hittite: thirty and seven in all” (2 Samuel 23:39). The second of the three follows at once: “And after him was Eleazar the son of Dodo the Ahohite, one of the three mighty men with David, when they defied the Philistines that were there gathered together to battle, and the men of Israel were gone away” (2 Samuel 23:9). An Eznite stood at the head of the men who held the field when Israel ran.

corruption_summary: The differences between 2 Samuel 23 and 1 Chronicles 11 are urged as proof of a broken text, where the Authorized Version renders both and flags the alternatives in its margin.
corruption_paragraphs: This verse is the standard exhibit for the claim that the Old Testament text has decayed beyond recovery: a different name for the chief, a different number of the slain, and a cluster of marginal variants. The honest account is narrower. Two inspired records of the same roll differ in a name and a figure; the Hebrew of 2 Samuel 23:8 is difficult; and the translators, far from hiding any of it, printed the alternative readings beside the text so that an English reader could see exactly where the difficulty lies. A version that shows its working is not the one to charge with concealment.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the doctrine of preservation concerns the text God has in fact given His church, difficulties and margins included, and not a text purged of every hard place for our comfort. The chapter's own point survives untouched: these men stood when Israel fled, and the list ends with Uriah.

pos: n. (chief among David's captains, who slew eight hundred at one time; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Adino, commonly explained as his ornament or his delight, from 'adan, to be luxuriant or delicate; named once, 2 Samuel 23:8.
biblical_def: Adino is named once, and stands first among David's warriors: “These be the names of the mighty men whom David had: The Tachmonite that sat in the seat, chief among the captains; the same was Adino the Eznite: he lift up his spear against eight hundred, whom he slew at one time” (2 Samuel 23:8). That sat in the seat marks an office and not a rest; he held the chief place among the captains. Chronicles records the same man at the head of the same roll under another name: “And this is the number of the mighty men whom David had; Jashobeam, an Hachmonite, the chief of the captains: he lifted up his spear against three hundred slain by him at one time” (1 Chronicles 11:11). The next rank is named in the same chapter: “And Abishai, the brother of Joab, the son of Zeruiah, was chief among three. And he lifted up his spear against three hundred, and slew them, and had the name among three” (2 Samuel 23:18); and the whole company is counted at the end: “Uriah the Hittite: thirty and seven in all” (2 Samuel 23:39). A man whose name means his delight is remembered for a single sentence about a spear. Scripture gives him no speech, no genealogy and no death; it gives him his post and his deed, and moves on.

corruption_summary: Numbers like eight hundred slain at one time are treated as heroic exaggeration, where Scripture reports the deeds of such men and names the one who gave the victory.
corruption_paragraphs: The usual handling of 2 Samuel 23 is to call it heroic saga, with the figures inflated as such literature inflates them. Two things should be weighed against that. First, the chapter is not written to praise the men: the same roll that honours them ends with Uriah the Hittite, whose name indicts the king who published the list. Second, the chapter itself attributes the victories to God, saying of the great day at Pas-dammim that “the LORD wrought a great victory” — the men are credited with standing, and God with the outcome.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the brevity of the record. Adino has one sentence; others have one word. Scripture does not flatter even its heroes with biographies, and it closes this roll with the name of a murdered man, so that no reader can finish the chapter admiring David without remembering what David did.

pos: n. (the designation of Paarai, one of David's thirty; named once)
etymology: A gentilic, Hebrew 'Arbi, a man of Arab, a town in the hill country of Judah named at Joshua 15:52; used once, 2 Samuel 23:35.
biblical_def: Arbite occurs once, near the end of the roll of the thirty: “Hezrai the Carmelite, Paarai the Arbite” (2 Samuel 23:35). The verse is four words of names and nothing else, which is how most of these men appear. Arab was a town of the Judean hill country, listed in Joshua's survey with Dumah and Eshean, so Paarai was a man of Judah's own back country. The Chronicles parallel gives a different name in the same place: “Hezro the Carmelite, Naarai the son of Ezbai” (1 Chronicles 11:37), and the dictionary records the difference without smoothing it. The roll he belongs to is counted plainly: “Uriah the Hittite: thirty and seven in all” (2 Samuel 23:39), and it includes the names of men who came from everywhere — Hittite, Ammonite, Moabite — and from every corner of Israel. The company began in a cave: these were the men who gathered to David when he was hunted, and the valiant men of the armies are listed beside them, “Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem” (1 Chronicles 11:26). A man from a small hill town stood in that company and is named for it.

corruption_summary: Lists of unknown soldiers are treated as filler, where Scripture preserves the name and town of every man who stood with David in his rejection.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern readers skip these verses and critical readers treat them as administrative debris. Both miss what a roll of names does. These men attached themselves to an anointed king while he was hunted, outlawed and living in caves, before there was a throne to gain by it; and when the throne came, their names were written down one by one, with the towns they came from. A list is the form that loyalty takes in a record. It is also the form the Holy Ghost chose for the register of the Lamb's own people.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour God puts on obscure faithfulness. Paarai the Arbite has four words in Scripture and no deed attached to his name, and he is in the book. The men who came to David in the cave are the pattern of those who confess Christ before He is seen to reign.

pos: n. (the designation of Hashem, whose sons were among David's mighty men; named once)
etymology: A gentilic of uncertain origin, Hebrew Gizoni, presumably from a place Gizon which Scripture does not elsewhere name; used once, 1 Chronicles 11:34.
biblical_def: Gizonite occurs once: “The sons of Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan the son of Shage the Hararite” (1 Chronicles 11:34). The place Gizon is nowhere else named in Scripture, and the dictionary does not supply it. The parallel in Samuel has a different reading at the same point in the list: “Eliahba the Shaalbonite, of the sons of Jashen, Jonathan” (2 Samuel 23:32), and the translators' margin at Chronicles notes Jashen as an alternative to Hashem. What stands in both is the notable fact that a father is honoured here through his sons: the register does not say Hashem the Gizonite alone but the sons of Hashem, so that more than one man of that household was counted among the mighty. The list is introduced as a roll of valiant men: “Also the valiant men of the armies were, Asahel the brother of Joab, Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem” (1 Chronicles 11:26), and it closes in Samuel with the total, “Uriah the Hittite: thirty and seven in all” (2 Samuel 23:39). An unknown town sent a household into David's company, and the household is named by its father.

corruption_summary: An unidentifiable place-name is used to argue the text is corrupt; the faithful course is to render what stands and admit the limit of what is known.
corruption_paragraphs: Gizon appears nowhere else, and the Samuel parallel reads differently, so this half-verse is regularly produced as evidence of textual decay and freely emended in modern treatments. The sober answer is that a place named once in Scripture and nowhere in surviving records is simply a place we do not know, which is true of a great many ancient towns. The Authorized Version renders the Hebrew of Chronicles and prints the variant in its margin, which is all a translation owes the reader and more than most give.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a household can be counted together. The register honours “the sons of Hashem,” not one man alone, which is how Scripture ordinarily speaks of covenant blessing: fathers and their houses, named together and standing together.

pos: n. (the designation of Keilah in the genealogies of Judah; named once)
etymology: A gentilic of uncertain origin, Hebrew Garmi, perhaps from gerem, a bone, and so bony or strong; used once, 1 Chronicles 4:19.
biblical_def: Garmite occurs once, in the crowded Judahite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4: “And the sons of his wife Hodiah the sister of Naham, the father of Keilah the Garmite, and Eshtemoa the Maachathite” (1 Chronicles 4:19). Keilah is also the name of a town in Judah that David once delivered from the Philistines and whose men would have given him up to Saul; here the name belongs to a man, or is used of the clan that held the town, which is the ordinary way of these registers. The chapter is a thicket of names, and the Authorized Version's margin notes Jehudijah as an alternative for Hodiah, the same woman named in the verse before: “And his wife Jehudijah bare Jered the father of Gedor, and Heber the father of Socho, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah” (1 Chronicles 4:18). In the middle of these lists stands one of the best-known prayers in Scripture: “And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested” (1 Chronicles 4:10).

corruption_summary: Jabez's prayer is lifted out of this genealogy and sold as a formula for material increase, where the man asks chiefly to be kept from evil.
corruption_paragraphs: The chapter that gives us the Garmite is best known for a prayer that has been detached from it, printed on its own, and marketed as a method for obtaining prosperity. The prayer itself has four petitions, and the weight falls on the last two: that God's hand might be with him, and that he might be kept from evil so that it would not grieve him. Enlarging a coast, in a book about tribal inheritance, means receiving what God has promised, not acquiring what a man has coveted. A petition torn from its register and turned into a technique has been made to say the opposite of what it says.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God hears obscure men in the middle of long lists. Jabez has two verses between two columns of names, and the chapter records plainly that God granted him what he asked. That is the encouragement a reader is meant to take from a genealogy.

pos: n. (the designation of Josabad, who came to David at Ziklag; named once)
etymology: A gentilic from Gederah, a town in the lowland of Judah named at Joshua 15:36; Hebrew Gederathi, from gader, a wall or hedge; used once, 1 Chronicles 12:4.
biblical_def: Gederathite occurs once, among the men who joined David before he was king: “And Ismaiah the Gibeonite, a mighty man among the thirty, and over the thirty; and Jeremiah, and Jahaziel, and Johanan, and Josabad the Gederathite” (1 Chronicles 12:4). Gederah was a town of the Judean lowland, and its name is simply the Hebrew word for a wall or sheepfold. The setting of the whole chapter is given in its first verse: “Now these are they that came to David to Ziklag, while he yet kept himself close because of Saul the son of Kish: and they were among the mighty men, helpers of the war” (1 Chronicles 12:1). The men of this company were Benjamites — Saul's own tribe — and ambidextrous bowmen: “They were armed with bows, and could use both the right hand and the left in hurling stones and shooting arrows out of a bow, even of Saul's brethren of Benjamin” (1 Chronicles 12:2). To leave Saul's house for a fugitive took more than skill, and the chapter records the word that settled it: “Then the spirit came upon Amasai, who was chief of the captains, and he said, Thine are we, David, and on thy side, thou son of Jesse: peace, peace be unto thee, and peace be to thine helpers; for thy God helpeth thee” (1 Chronicles 12:18).

corruption_summary: David's following is described as a warband assembled by ambition, where Chronicles presents men leaving their own tribe's king for one God had anointed.
corruption_paragraphs: A political reading of 1 Chronicles 12 sees a rising strongman gathering fighters who sensed where advantage lay. The chapter's details make that hard to sustain. These were Benjamites, Saul's kinsmen, joining a man with no throne, no city and no prospect, who “yet kept himself close because of Saul” (1 Chronicles 12:1). What they confess through Amasai is not calculation but conviction: “for thy God helpeth thee” (1 Chronicles 12:18). The chapter attributes the whole movement to the Spirit coming upon a captain, not to a reading of the odds.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that faith commits before it can see. A man of Gederah left the lowland of Judah for a cave, and Scripture keeps his town in his name. Those who come to the Lord's Anointed while He is still rejected are the ones named in the registers of His reign.

pos: n. (the designation of Shammah and Elika, two of David's thirty; named twice)
etymology: A gentilic, Hebrew Charodi, presumably from Harod, the spring where Gideon's army was sifted; used twice in one verse, 2 Samuel 23:25.
biblical_def: Harodite stands twice in a single verse of the roll of the thirty: “Shammah the Harodite, Elika the Harodite” (2 Samuel 23:25). Two men of one town were counted among David's mighty men, which is a small honour to a small place. The town is presumably that of the well of Harod, beside which Gideon's thirty-two thousand were reduced to three hundred. The Chronicles parallel gives the form Harorite and a slightly different name, and its margin notes both: “Shammoth the Harorite, Helez the Pelonite” (1 Chronicles 11:27). The verse before in Samuel sets the company: “Asahel the brother of Joab was one of the thirty; Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem” (2 Samuel 23:24), and the roll is counted at its end: “Uriah the Hittite: thirty and seven in all” (2 Samuel 23:39). The Authorized Version keeps Harodite in Samuel and Harorite in Chronicles because that is what the two books have, and prints the alternative in the margin where the Hebrew allows it. The dictionary follows the same practice, naming Harorite inside this entry rather than making a second one.

corruption_summary: Parallel rolls that differ in a letter are made the ground of a general distrust of Scripture, where the difference is a known feature of the text and is printed openly.
corruption_paragraphs: Harodite in Samuel and Harorite in Chronicles differ by a single consonant, and such pairs are gathered by the thousand into arguments that the Old Testament cannot be trusted. The argument needs the pairs to matter, and they do not. No doctrine, no history and no promise turns on which letter stands in a gentilic; the two books agree that two men of one small town were in the company; and the translators printed the variant in the margin rather than choosing silently between them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that two men came out of Harod. If the town is Gideon's spring, then the place where an army was cut to three hundred afterwards sent two of the thirty-seven to David — and the God who had refused numbers there was pleased to name individuals here.

pos: n. (the designation of Shemaah, whose sons came to David at Ziklag; named once)
etymology: A gentilic from Gibeah, Hebrew Gib'athi, from gib'ah, a hill; used once, 1 Chronicles 12:3.
biblical_def: Gibeathite occurs once: “The chief was Ahiezer, then Joash, the sons of Shemaah the Gibeathite; and Jeziel, and Pelet, the sons of Azmaveth; and Berachah, and Jehu the Antothite” (1 Chronicles 12:3). Gibeah was Saul's own town, which gives the verse its force: the two leading men in this company came from the king's city and went over to the fugitive. The chapter says as much: these were Benjamites, “even of Saul's brethren of Benjamin” (1 Chronicles 12:2), and they were skilled with either hand at bow and sling. The occasion is stated at the head of the chapter: “Now these are they that came to David to Ziklag, while he yet kept himself close because of Saul the son of Kish” (1 Chronicles 12:1). David's response, when the Spirit moved their captain to swear loyalty, was to receive them without a test: “Then David received them, and made them captains of the band” (1 Chronicles 12:18). Gibeah is a name with a dark history in Israel, for the outrage that nearly destroyed Benjamin happened there; and here men of Gibeah are the first named among those who came to the Lord's anointed in his rejection.

corruption_summary: Defection from Saul to David is judged by the standards of political loyalty, where Scripture judges it by the question of whom God had anointed.
corruption_paragraphs: Men of Saul's own tribe and town leaving him for David is read, naturally enough, as treachery or as opportunism. Scripture frames it otherwise. Saul had been rejected from being king by the word of the LORD through Samuel; David had been anointed by the same prophet; and the question before every Israelite was not which man would win but which man God had chosen. The chapter credits the decision to the Spirit and not to calculation, and it records that the men came while David was still hiding.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that lawful authority rests on God's appointment and not on possession. Gibeah had been the scene of Israel's worst hour and was the seat of a rejected king; and out of Gibeah came the chief of the men who crossed over. Grace reaches a town with a bad name.

pos: n. (a native of Bethlehem; used of Jesse, and of Elhanan)
etymology: A gentilic from Bethlehem, Hebrew Beth-lechem, house of bread; used of Jesse the father of David, 1 Samuel 16:1, 16:18, 17:58.
biblical_def: Bethlehemite is the word by which Scripture marks out the family from which the king came. It is used first in the LORD's commission to Samuel: “And the LORD said unto Samuel, How long wilt thou mourn for Saul, seeing I have rejected him from reigning over Israel? fill thine horn with oil, and go, I will send thee to Jesse the Bethlehemite: for I have provided me a king among his sons” (1 Samuel 16:1). It is used again when David is first commended at court: “Then answered one of the servants, and said, Behold, I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, that is cunning in playing, and a mighty valiant man, and a man of war, and prudent in matters, and a comely person, and the LORD is with him” (1 Samuel 16:18). And it is in David's own mouth when Saul asks whose son he is after Goliath falls: “And Saul said to him, Whose son art thou, thou young man? And David answered, I am the son of thy servant Jesse the Bethlehemite” (1 Samuel 17:58). The town is small and the name is a prophecy: “But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting” (Micah 5:2). House of Bread sent Israel a shepherd-king, and sent the world the Bread of Life.

corruption_summary: Micah's prophecy is explained as a later reading-back from the Gospels, where the text stands in the prophets centuries before and asserts the Ruler's eternity.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard critical handling of Micah 5:2 is to treat the Bethlehem prophecy as a Christian retrojection, or to read it as a general hope for a Davidic restoration with the town supplied afterwards. The verse resists both. It names the place, states its insignificance, and then says of the one who comes out of it that his “goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting” — a claim no merely Davidic hope requires and no later editor would invent in that form. The chief priests of Herod's day, who had no interest in helping Christians, answered the question from this verse without hesitation.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pattern God keeps. He sent His prophet past the tall son and the strong son to the one keeping sheep; He chose the little town among the thousands of Judah; and He laid His own Son in a manger there. The gentilic that marks Jesse marks the whole method of God's choosing.

pos: n. (the designation of Elihu, the fourth speaker in Job; named twice)
etymology: A gentilic from Buz, Hebrew Buzi; Buz was a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and the name also belongs to a people of the east; used twice, Job 32:2 and 32:6.
biblical_def: Buzite is the designation of Elihu, who had sat silent through the long dispute and then spoke: “Then was kindled the wrath of Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram: against Job was his wrath kindled, because he justified himself rather than God” (Job 32:2). He gives his own reason for waiting: “And Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said, I am young, and ye are very old; wherefore I was afraid, and durst not shew you mine opinion” (Job 32:6). His argument turns on a principle he states at once, that age is not the source of understanding: “But there is a spirit in man: and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding” (Job 32:8). Elihu is the one speaker in the book whom God does not rebuke. The three friends are named and censured by the LORD Himself at the end: “And it was so, that after the LORD had spoken these words unto Job, the LORD said to Eliphaz the Temanite, My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath” (Job 42:7). Elihu is not in that sentence, and his speeches turn the book from the friends' accusations toward the greatness of God, which is the subject of the whirlwind.

corruption_summary: The Elihu speeches are called a later insertion, and his argument lumped in with the friends', where the LORD's own rebuke at the end names the three and passes him by.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical treatments of Job commonly excise chapters 32 to 37 as a later addition, on the ground that Elihu appears without introduction and is never answered. The book is composed to make that reading unlikely. Elihu's silence is explained in the text by his youth; his entrance prepares the whirlwind by turning the subject from Job's case to God's greatness and God's teaching through affliction; and when the LORD apportions blame He names Eliphaz and “thy two friends” (Job 42:7) and says nothing against Elihu. An interpolation would be the easiest thing to condemn, and the text does not condemn it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Elihu states: understanding is not a function of years but a gift, for “there is a spirit in man: and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding” (Job 32:8). A young man waited his turn, honoured his elders, and then said what none of them had said.
